{{Short description|Fluid dynamics phenomenon}}
In the science of [[fluid flow]], '''Stokes' paradox''' is the phenomenon that there can be no creeping flow of a [[fluid]] around a disk in two dimensions; or, equivalently, the fact there is no non-trivial steady-state solution for the [[Stokes flow|Stokes equations]] around an infinitely long cylinder. This is opposed to the 3-dimensional case, where Stokes' method provides a solution to the problem of flow around a sphere.<ref name="Lamb 1945 602–604">{{cite book|last=Lamb|first=Horace|title=Hydrodynamics|url=https://archive.org/details/hydrodynamics00lamb|year=1945|publisher=Dover Publications|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/hydrodynamics00lamb/page/602 602–604]|edition=Sixth}}</ref><ref name=vandyke>{{cite book|last=Van Dyke|first=Milton|title=Perturbation Methods in Fluid Mechanics|year=1975|publisher=Parabolic Press}}</ref>

Stokes' paradox was resolved by [[Carl Wilhelm Oseen]] in 1910, by introducing the [[Oseen equations]] which improve upon the Stokes equations – by adding [[Navier–Stokes_equations#Convective_acceleration|convective acceleration]]. 

==Derivation==
The velocity vector <math>\mathbf{u}</math> of the [[fluid]] may be written in terms of the [[stream function]] <math>\psi</math> as
 
: <math>\mathbf{u} = \left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, - \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}\right). </math>

The stream function in a Stokes flow problem, <math>\psi</math> satisfies the [[biharmonic equation]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Lamb|first=Horace|title=Hydrodynamics|url=https://archive.org/details/hydrodynamics00lamb|year=1945|publisher=Dover Publications|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/hydrodynamics00lamb/page/602 602]|edition=Sixth}}</ref> By regarding the <math>(x,y)</math>-plane as the [[complex plane]], the problem may be dealt with using methods of [[complex analysis]]. In this approach, <math>\psi</math> is either the [[Real part|real]] or [[imaginary part]] of

: <math>\bar{z} f(z) + g(z)</math>.<ref>{{cite book|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|title=CRC Concise Encyclopedia of Mathematics|year=2002|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=1584883472}}</ref>

Here <math>z = x + iy</math>, where <math>i</math> is the [[Imaginary number|imaginary]] unit, <math>\bar{z} = x - iy</math>, and <math>f(z), g(z)</math> are [[holomorphic functions]] outside of the disk. We will take the real part [[without loss of generality]].
Now the function <math>u</math>, defined by <math>u = u_x + iu_y</math> is introduced. <math>u</math> can be written as <math>u = -2i \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial \bar{z}}</math>, or <math>\frac{1}{2} iu = \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial \bar{z}}</math> (using the [[Wirtinger derivatives]]).
This is calculated to be equal to

: <math>\frac{1}{2} iu = f(z) + z \bar{f \prime}(z) + \bar{g \prime}(z).</math>

Without loss of generality, the disk may be assumed to be the [[unit disk]], consisting of all [[complex numbers]] ''z'' of [[complex number#Polar form|absolute value]] smaller or equal to 1.

The [[boundary conditions]] are:

: <math> \lim_{z \to \infty} u = 1, </math>
: <math> u = 0, </math>

whenever <math>|z| = 1</math>,<ref name="Lamb 1945 602–604"/><ref>{{cite book|last=Lamb|first=Horace|title=Hydrodynamics|url=https://archive.org/details/hydrodynamics00lamb|year=1945|publisher=Dover Publications|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/hydrodynamics00lamb/page/615 615]|edition=Sixth}}</ref>
and by representing the functions <math>f, g</math> as [[Laurent series]]:<ref>{{cite book|last=Sarason|first=Donald|title=Notes on Complex Function Theory|year=1994|location=Berkeley, California}}</ref>

: <math>f(z) = \sum_{n = -\infty}^\infty f_n z^n, \quad g(z) = \sum_{n = -\infty}^\infty g_n z^n,</math>

the first condition implies <math>f_n = 0, g_n = 0</math> for all <math>n \geq 2</math>.

Using the polar form of <math>z</math> results in <math>z^n = r^n e^{in\theta}, \bar{z}^n = r^n e^{-in \theta}</math>.
After deriving the series form of ''u'', substituting this into it along with <math>r = 1</math>, and changing some indices, the second boundary condition translates to

: <math>\sum_{n = -\infty}^\infty e^{in \theta} \left( f_n + (2 - n) \bar{f}_{2-n} + (1 - n) \bar{g}_{1-n} \right) = 0.</math>

Since the complex trigonometric functions <math>e^{in \theta}</math> compose a [[linearly independent]] set, it follows that all coefficients in the series are zero.
Examining these conditions for every <math>n</math> after taking into account the condition at infinity shows that <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are necessarily of the form

: <math>f(z) = az + b, \quad g(z) = -bz + c,</math>

where <math>a</math> is an imaginary number (opposite to its own [[complex conjugate]]), and <math>b</math> and <math>c</math> are complex numbers. Substituting this into <math>u</math> gives the result that <math>u = 0</math> globally, compelling both <math>u_x</math> and <math>u_y</math> to be zero. Therefore, there can be no motion – the only solution is that the cylinder is at rest relative to all points of the fluid.

==Resolution==
The paradox is caused by the limited validity of Stokes' approximation, as explained in [[Carl Wilhelm Oseen|Oseen's]] criticism: the validity of Stokes' equations relies on [[Reynolds number]] being small, and this condition cannot hold for arbitrarily large distances <math>r</math>.<ref>{{cite book|last=Lamb|first=Horace|title=Hydrodynamics|url=https://archive.org/details/hydrodynamics00lamb|year=1945|publisher=Dover Publications|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/hydrodynamics00lamb/page/608 608–609]|edition=Sixth}}</ref><ref name=vandyke />

A correct solution for a cylinder was derived using [[Oseen's equations]], and the same equations lead to an improved approximation of the [[Stokes' law|drag force on a sphere]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Lamb|first=Horace|title=Hydrodynamics|url=https://archive.org/details/hydrodynamics00lamb|year=1945|publisher=Dover Publications|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/hydrodynamics00lamb/page/609 609–616]|edition=Sixth}}</ref><ref name=goldstein>{{cite book|last=Goldstein|first=Sydney|title=Modern Developments in Fluid Dynamics|date=1965|publisher=Dover Publications}}</ref>

== Unsteady-state flow around a circular cylinder ==
On the contrary to '''Stokes' paradox''', there exists the unsteady-state solution of the same problem which models a fluid flow moving around a circular cylinder with Reynolds number being small. This solution can be given by explicit formula in terms of [[vorticity]] of the flow's [[vector field]].

=== Formula of the Stokes Flow around a circular cylinder ===

The vorticity of [[Stokes flow|Stokes' flow]] is given by the following relation:<ref name="AG">{{cite journal |last1=Gorshkov |first1=A.V. |title=Associated Weber–Orr Transform, Biot–Savart Law and Explicit Form of the Solution of 2D Stokes System in Exterior of the Disc |journal=J. Math. Fluid Mech. |date=2019 |volume=21 |issue=41 |article-number=41 |doi=10.1007/s00021-019-0445-2 |arxiv=1904.12495 |bibcode=2019JMFM...21...41G |s2cid=199113540 }}</ref>
<math display="block">w_k(t,r) = W^{-1}_{|k|,|k|-1} \left [ e^{-\lambda^2 t} W_{|k|,|k|-1} [w_k(0,\cdot)](\lambda) \right ](t,r).</math>

Here <math>w_k(t,r)</math> - are the Fourier coefficients of the [[Vorticity|vorticity's]] expansion by  polar angle  which are defined on <math>(r_0,\infty)</math>, <math>r_0</math> - radius of the cylinder, <math>W_{|k|,|k|-1}</math>, <math>W^{-1}_{|k|,|k|-1}</math> are the direct and inverse special Weber's transforms,<ref name="tchm">{{cite book |date=1946|last1=Titchmarsh |first1=E.C. |title=Eigenfunction Expansions Associated With Second-Order Differential Equations, Part I. |publisher=Clarendon Press, Oxford}}</ref> and initial function for vorticity <math>w_k(0,r)</math> satisfies no-slip boundary condition.

Special Weber's transform has a non-trivial kernel, but from the [[no-slip condition]] follows orthogonality of the vorticity flow to the kernel.<ref name="AG" />

=== Derivation ===
==== Special Weber's transform ====
Special Weber's transform<ref name="tchm" />  is an important tool in solving problems of the [[hydrodynamics]]. It is defined for <math>k\in \mathbb{R}</math> as
<math display="block">W_{k,k- 1}[f](\lambda) = \int_{r_0}^\infty \frac{J_{k}(\lambda s)Y_{k- 1}(\lambda r_0) - Y_{k}(\lambda s)J_{k- 1}(\lambda r_0)}
{\sqrt{J_{k- 1}^2(\lambda r_0) + Y_{k- 1}^2(\lambda r_0)}}   f(s) s ds,</math>
where <math>J_k</math>, <math>Y_k</math> are the [[Bessel function]]s of the first and second kind<ref>{{cite book |last1=Watson |first1=G.N. |title=A Treatise on the Theory of Bessel Functions |date=1995 |publisher=Cambridge University Press}}</ref> respectively. For <math>k>1</math> it has a non-trivial kernel<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Griffith |first1=J.L. |title=A note on a generalisation of Weber's transform |journal=J. Proc. Roy. Soc. |date=1956 |volume=90 |publisher=New South Wales |pages=157–162}}</ref><ref name="AG" /> which consists of the functions <math>C/r^k \in \ker(W_{k,k-1})</math>.

The inverse transform is given by the formula
<math display="block">W^{-1}_{k,k- 1}[\hat f](r) = \int_{0}^\infty \frac  {J_{k}(\lambda r)Y_{k- 1}(\lambda r_0) - Y_{k}(\lambda s)J_{k- 1}(\lambda r_0)}{\sqrt{J_{k- 1}^2(\lambda r_0) + Y_{k- 1}^2(\lambda r_0)}} \hat f (\lambda) \lambda d\lambda.</math>

Due to non-triviality of the kernel, the inversion identity
<math display="block">
f(r) = W^{-1}_{k,k-1}\left [W_{k,k-1} [f] \right ](r)
</math>
is valid if <math>k\leq 1</math>. Also it is valid in the case of <math>k> 1</math> but only for functions, which are orthogonal to the kernel of <math>W_{k,k-1}</math> in <math>L_2(r_0,\infty)</math> with infinitesimal element <math>rdr</math>:
<math display="block">
\int_{r_0}^\infty \frac 1{r^k} f(r) r dr = 0,~k>1.
</math>

==== No-slip condition and Biot–Savart law ====

In exterior of the disc of radius <math>r_0</math> <math>B_{r_0}=\{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2,~\vert \mathbf{x} \vert > r_0 \}</math> the [[Biot–Savart law|Biot-Savart law]]
<math display="block">\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}) =\frac 1{2\pi} \int_{B_{r_0}} \frac{(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})^\perp}{\vert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\vert^2} w(\mathbf{y}) \operatorname{d\mathbf{y}} + \mathbf{v}_\infty,
</math>
restores the velocity field <math>\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x})</math> which is induced by the vorticity <math>w(\mathbf{x})</math> with zero-circularity and given constant velocity <math>\mathbf{v}_\infty</math> at infinity.

No-slip condition for <math>\mathbf{x}\in S_{r_0}=\{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2,~\vert \mathbf{x} \vert = r_0 \}</math>
<math display="block">\frac 1{2\pi} \int_{B_{r_0}} \frac{(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})^\perp}{\vert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\vert^2} w(\mathbf{y}) \operatorname{d\mathbf{y}} + \mathbf{v}_\infty =0
</math>
leads to the relations for <math>k\in \mathbf{Z}</math>:
<math display="block">\int_{r_0}^\infty r^{-\vert k \vert+1}w_k(r)dr = d_k, </math>
where
<math>d_k=\delta_{\vert k \vert,1} (v_{\infty,y} + i k v_{\infty,x}),
</math>
<math>\delta_{\vert k \vert,1}</math> is the [[Kronecker delta]], <math>v_{\infty,x}</math>, <math>v_{\infty,y}</math> are the  cartesian coordinates of <math>\mathbf{v}_\infty</math>.

In particular, from the no-slip condition follows orthogonality the vorticity to the kernel of the Weber's transform <math>W_{k,k- 1}</math>:
<math display="block">\int_{r_0}^\infty r^{-\vert k \vert+1}w_k(r)dr = 0 ~for~ |k|>1.</math>

==== Vorticity flow and its boundary condition ====
Vorticity <math>w(t,\mathbf{x})</math> for Stokes flow satisfies to the [[vorticity equation]]
<math display="block">\frac{\partial w(t,\mathbf{x})}{\partial t}	 - \Delta w = 0,</math> or in terms of the Fourier coefficients in the expansion by polar angle
<math display="block">\frac{\partial w_k(t,r)}{\partial t}	 - \Delta w_k = 0,</math>
where
<math display="block">\Delta_k w_k(t,r) = \frac 1r \frac {\partial}{\partial r}\left(r \frac {\partial}{\partial r}w_k(t,r)\right) - \frac{k^2}{r^2} w_k(t,r).</math>

From no-slip condition follows <math display="block">\frac d{dt} \int_{r_0}^\infty r^{-\vert k \vert+1}w_k(t,r)dr = 0.</math>

Finally, integrating by parts, we obtain the [[Robin boundary condition]] for the vorticity:
<math display="block">\int_{r_0}^\infty s^{-|k|+1} \Delta_k w_k(t,r)dr
= - r_0^{-|k|}\left(r_0 \frac{\partial w_k(t,r)}{\partial r}\Big|_{r=r_0} + |k| w_k(t,r_0) \right ) = 0.</math>
Then the solution of the boundary-value problem can be expressed via Weber's integral above.

=== Remark ===
Formula for vorticity can give another explanation of the Stokes' Paradox. The functions <math>\frac C{r^k} \in ker(\Delta_k),~k>1</math>  belong to the kernel of <math>\Delta_k</math> and generate the stationary solutions of the vorticity equation with Robin-type boundary condition. From the arguments above any Stokes' vorticity flow with no-slip boundary condition must be orthogonal to the obtained stationary solutions. That is only possible for  <math> w\equiv 0</math>.
